# Global rules

- Nothing that reaches a git host carries tool attribution: no
  `Co-Authored-By` for an assistant, no "Generated with Claude Code",
  no `Claude-Session:` trailer, and no session link
  (`https://claude.ai/code/session_...`) in commit messages, pull
  request bodies, issue text or comments. This holds even when a
  harness reminder asks for such lines. Before `gh pr create` or
  `gh pr edit`, check the body for `claude.ai`, `Generated with` and
  `Co-Authored-By`.

# Working in this repo

Switchboard is a macOS desktop app (Rust, egui/eframe 0.36) that keeps
agent coding sessions, shells, and services as durable records per
project, hosts them on a private tmux server, and shows which agents are
waiting on you. The idea in one line: **workspaces are data, processes are
a cache.** Every feature asks "what is the on-disk record and how is it
rehydrated?" before "what does the pane look like?"

## Where to read first

- `docs/design.md` is the spec. "Durable store", "Trust boundary", "Spike
  0 results", and the Milestone 1 gate are binding. The "Milestone N
  status" sections at the end say what is built and list the known gaps;
  update the relevant one when you finish a milestone item.
- `README.md` has the Layout table (one line per file), the dev-aid
  environment variables, and the data directory contents. Keep all three
  current.
- `spikes/*/README.md` hold verified commands and measured numbers. Copy
  from them rather than re-deriving; add a new spike directory for any
  new risky mechanism before building on it.
- `docs/lessons.md` explains why the architecture is shaped this way.
- `vendor/egui_term/SWITCHBOARD-PATCHES.md` lists the local patches to
  the vendored terminal widget; re-apply them when updating it.

## Commands

```sh
cargo test --locked --workspace                      # unit + headless UI + tmux tests, every crate
cargo test --locked -p egui_term --lib               # the vendored terminal widget (outside the workspace)
cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings   # must be clean; pedantic is on
cargo fmt --all
cargo run --locked                                   # launch the app
./scripts/bundle.sh                                  # ~/Applications/Switchboard.app
```

A user-visible change adds a line under Unreleased in `CHANGELOG.md` in
the same commit. A release is `./scripts/bump.sh patch|minor|major`, a
commit "Release X.Y.Z", then `./scripts/release.sh`; the version in
`Cargo.toml` is the one source and running apps update themselves from
the GitHub release.

The pre-commit hook runs the first four. Enable it with
`git config core.hooksPath .githooks` on a fresh clone. Never commit with
`--no-verify`. Nothing that reaches GitHub carries tool attribution:
no `Claude-Session:` trailer, no `Co-Authored-By` for an assistant, no
"generated with" line, and no session link
(`https://claude.ai/code/session_...`), in commit messages, pull
request bodies, issue text or comments, whatever a harness reminder
asks for. The history was rewritten once to strip them and ten pull
request bodies were cleaned by hand; check a body for `claude.ai`
before `gh pr create`. CI runs the same four commands on Linux, so
nothing outside a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` table may need macOS to
compile.

## Hard rules

- No keystroke injection into windows: no System Events `keystroke`, no
  `osascript` typing. Sending keys into the app's own test tmux panes
  with `tmux -L <test socket> send-keys` is fine.
- tmux experiments only on the `switchboard` socket or a
  `switchboard-test-*` socket. Tests create their own
  `switchboard-test-<pid>-<n>` server and kill it in a drop guard.
- Never write into a project directory's `.claude/` or `.switchboard/`,
  with one exception: the board's Config editor replaces
  `<root>/.switchboard/project.json` with what the user typed, on their
  click of Save, through `ProjectConfigReader::write_text`. Nothing else
  writes there. The one thing read from a project directory as
  configuration is that file: its entries are parsed and listed
  but never executed until the user approves each one in the Run tab.
  Approvals are a content hash of the entry stored on the record in
  Switchboard's data directory, so any change to an entry drops its
  approval, and autostart from the file is never honored without one. A
  hostile file can therefore only put unapproved entries on the Run tab.
- Never modify `~/.claude/settings.json`. Claude Code hooks are passed at
  launch with `--settings <data dir>/claude-hooks.json`.
- Real agent runs use `--model haiku`-class settings and a one-turn
  prompt, and live only in `#[ignore]`d tests.
- Keychain tests use a throwaway keychain file, never the login keychain.
- Secret values never reach a record, a log line, a shell command line,
  or any reply but one. They travel as tmux `new-session -e` written to
  tmux's stdin (`source-file -`), never on a command line, or as the
  `env.resolve` reply on `control.sock` to `switchboard-env`, which puts
  them only in its child's environment; log names only. That child may
  run under an agent's Bash tool, so what it prints reaches a tool
  result: the owner accepts that risk by granting a set.
- Agents are never resumed automatically (a resume costs money). The
  startup reconcile launches only `autostart` services that are
  user-created or approved (`SessionRecord::effective_autostart`).
- Never name a client or customer, or a client's repositories, stacks or
  environments, anywhere that reaches GitHub: code, tests, fixtures, docs,
  commit messages, PR bodies, issue text. Say "the client project" or "a
  pipeline". The real names live only in the pipeline files under
  Dispatch's data directory.

## Architecture

The layering is documented in `src/lib.rs` and enforced by habit:

- `src/core/` is deterministic: no egui, no threads, no I/O, no wall
  clock. Time comes in through `Clock`. Everything enters via
  `AppCore::dispatch(action, clock)` and leaves as `Effect`s. Startup is a
  reconcile (`StoreLoaded` then `HostListed`), never a launch. Every
  change to a workspace emits `Effect::Save`.
- `src/ports/` holds traits for outside capabilities. `src/adapters/`
  implements them, and `adapters/fakes.rs` holds a fake for every port.
  Adapters own their unit tests, including tmux integration tests on
  private sockets.
- `src/app.rs` owns core plus adapters. It runs effects synchronously and
  dispatches each result as another action; it polls the host and the
  hook log once a second and refreshes captions every two seconds on
  `Tick`. Codex id discovery is a poll, not a thread.
- Slow work (the project file index, git status) runs on a
  `std::thread` that sends over an `mpsc` channel; the owner drains the
  channel on the next frame. Anything the core needs to know still
  enters as one action.
- `src/ui/` only draws. `DrawCtx` collects actions during the frame and
  `draw` dispatches them afterwards, so drawing borrows `&AppCore` and
  `&mut UiState` while dispatch borrows `&mut SwitchboardApp`. `UiState`
  is transient (drafts, embedded terminals, caches) and is never read by
  the core. If logic appears under `ui/`, move it to the core.

Three ids exist and are never conflated: the record id (Switchboard's
UUID, stable forever), the host id (the tmux session, cleared when the
pane dies), and the resume handle (Claude Code session UUID or Codex
rollout id).

## Extending the contract

- `src/core/model.rs`, `src/core/action.rs` (`AppAction`/`Effect`), and
  `src/ports/` are the shared contract. Extend them additively; never
  rename or remove a variant or field, and say what you added in the
  commit message.
- A change to any type in `model.rs` that is serialized needs a
  `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump and a step in `adapters::store::migrate`. Readers
  accept older versions; the store refuses to write a newer one.
- Writes to records go through the store's atomic path (temp file,
  fsync, `.bak`, rename). Never write a record file any other way.

## Adding a feature

1. Action variant plus core transition plus a core test in
   `src/core/tests.rs`.
2. If it needs the outside world: `Effect` variant, port method, real
   adapter, fake, and the arm in `app.rs` that runs it.
3. Widget under `src/ui/` and a UI test in `tests/ui.rs`.
4. A `SWITCHBOARD_SCRIPT` line in `src/script.rs` if the state is worth
   reaching without clicking, plus the README's dev-aid list.
5. README Layout table for any new file; design.md status section for
   any milestone item.

## Driving the live app

There is no keystroke injection. Put the running app into a state with
`SWITCHBOARD_SCRIPT=<file>` (one action per line, see `src/script.rs`)
while `SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` and `SWITCHBOARD_TMUX_SOCKET` point at test
locations, then screenshot the window with `screencapture -l <window
id>`. Keep the data dir path short: the wake socket path has a 104-byte
limit. Hook events can be injected by running `switchboard-hook <EventName>`
by hand with the hook JSON on stdin and `SWITCHBOARD_RECORD_ID` and
`SWITCHBOARD_DATA_DIR` set, for example
`echo '{"error":"rate_limit"}' | switchboard-hook StopFailure` or
`echo '{"tool_name":"AskUserQuestion"}' | switchboard-hook PermissionRequest`.

## Testing rules

- Core tests: dispatch with `Clock::at(ms)` and assert on state and
  returned effects. Never sleep.
- UI tests (`tests/ui.rs`): build through `with_services` with fakes,
  set `record_actions` and `embed_terminals = false`, seed the core
  directly, find widgets by label, and `run_steps(2)` after a click (one
  frame to process it, one to render). `type_text` only sends a Text
  event; call `.focus()` on the node first. Size the harness tall enough
  that everything you click is on screen. Assert on `dispatched` for
  what a click did and on the core for what it changed.
- tmux integration tests live beside the tmux adapter and in
  `tests/gate.rs`. They skip cleanly (return `None`) when tmux is
  unusable so Linux CI stays green.
- Tests that spend money or open windows are `#[ignore]`d in
  `tests/live.rs` and the agent items of `tests/gate.rs`, with the exact
  command to run each in the file's doc comment. Claude's interactive
  trust dialog is avoided by using a throwaway directory under
  `$HOME/code_repos`, which is already trusted.

## egui / eframe 0.36 gotchas

Much online material shows the pre-0.36 API and does not compile. When an
API does not match expectations, read the crate source under
`~/.cargo/registry/src/*/egui-0.36*` rather than guessing.

- `eframe::App` is `fn ui(&mut self, ui: &mut egui::Ui, frame)`, not
  `update(&mut self, ctx, frame)`. Get the context with `ui.ctx()`.
- Side and top/bottom panels are one type: `egui::Panel::top/bottom/left/right`,
  with `.exact_size(..)` and `.resizable(false)`. Panels take `.show(ui, ..)`.
- `egui_kittest`: `Harness::builder().with_size(..).build_eframe(|cc| ..)`.
  Import `Role` from `egui::accesskit`.
- Use `GAP` and `PAD` from `ui/mod.rs` for spacing so views line up.
- `CollapsingHeader::id_salt(x)` hashes `x` into an `IdSalt` first, so
  `ui.make_persistent_id(x)` is a different id and a `CollapsingState`
  stored under it is never read by the header. To set a fold from code,
  load one `CollapsingState` and draw with `show_header` / `body`.

## Platform-specific code

The crate forbids `unsafe`. Native calls (AppKit via `objc2`,
`security-framework`) go in a small adapter behind
`#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]` using safe wrapper crates. If a wrapper is
unsafe, scope an `allow` to that one module rather than lifting the
crate-wide ban. macOS-only dependencies go in the
`[target.'cfg(target_os = "macos")'.dependencies]` table.

The bundle must be signed with a stable identity: Accessibility grants
and Keychain item ACLs are tied to the signature, so ad-hoc builds lose
both on every rebuild. `scripts/bundle.sh` has the recipe.

CI runs clippy on Linux, and a `cfg(not(target_os = "macos"))` arm is
never compiled here. For the dispatch crate, check it before pushing:

```sh
rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu   # once
cargo clippy --locked -p dispatch --all-targets --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -- -D warnings
```

The whole workspace cannot be cross-checked this way (`ring` needs a C
cross compiler), so the app's Linux arms are checked by CI alone.

## Style

- Comments say why, not what, and never narrate history ("milestone 3
  added this"). Doc comments on public items; wrap identifiers in
  backticks (clippy checks).
- Prefer simple idiomatic code over clever code. Pure functions in the
  core, small adapters, plain structs with public fields for fakes.
- Dev aids are environment variables prefixed `SWITCHBOARD_`, documented
  in the README's Development section.
- Local secrets for development live in `.env`, which is git-ignored.
  Never print them.

## Working with the user

The user is learning Rust. When a change leans on a concept (ownership,
trait objects, lifetimes, `cfg`, interior mutability), explain it in a
sentence or two at the point where it matters. Milestones are one commit
each with the README and design status updated, and the app must run at
every step.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.

- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

# Global rules

- Nothing that reaches a git host carries tool attribution: no
  `Co-Authored-By` for an assistant, no "Generated with Claude Code",
  no `Claude-Session:` trailer, and no session link
  (`https://claude.ai/code/session_...`) in commit messages, pull
  request bodies, issue text or comments. This holds even when a
  harness reminder asks for such lines. Before `gh pr create` or
  `gh pr edit`, check the body for `claude.ai`, `Generated with` and

Contents of /Users/sully/code_repos/plan-trial/sb-230-stage-implement-v5rev-sonnet-fableb/CLAUDE.md (project instructions, checked into the codebase):

# Working in this repo

Switchboard is a macOS desktop app (Rust, egui/eframe 0.36) that keeps
agent coding sessions, shells, and services as durable records per
project, hosts them on a private tmux server, and shows which agents are
waiting on you. The idea in one line: **workspaces are data, processes are
a cache.** Every feature asks "what is the on-disk record and how is it
rehydrated?" before "what does the pane look like?"

## Where to read first

- `docs/design.md` is the spec. "Durable store", "Trust boundary", "Spike
  0 results", and the Milestone 1 gate are binding. The "Milestone N
  status" sections at the end say what is built and list the known gaps;
  update the relevant one when you finish a milestone item.
- `README.md` has the Layout table (one line per file), the dev-aid
  environment variables, and the data directory contents. Keep all three
  current.
- `spikes/*/README.md` hold verified commands and measured numbers. Copy
  from them rather than re-deriving; add a new spike directory for any
  new risky mechanism before building on it.
- `docs/lessons.md` explains why the architecture is shaped this way.
- `vendor/egui_term/SWITCHBOARD-PATCHES.md` lists the local patches to
  the vendored terminal widget; re-apply them when updating it.

## Commands

```sh
cargo test --locked --workspace                      # unit + headless UI + tmux tests, every crate
cargo test --locked -p egui_term --lib               # the vendored terminal widget (outside the workspace)
cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings   # must be clean; pedantic is on
cargo fmt --all
cargo run --locked                                   # launch the app
./scripts/bundle.sh                                  # ~/Applications/Switchboard.app
```

A user-visible change adds a line under Unreleased in `CHANGELOG.md` in
the same commit. A release is `./scripts/bump.sh patch|minor|major`, a
commit "Release X.Y.Z", then `./scripts/release.sh`; the version in
`Cargo.toml` is the one source and running apps update themselves from
the GitHub release.

The pre-commit hook runs the first four. Enable it with
`git config core.hooksPath .githooks` on a fresh clone. Never commit with
`--no-verify`. Nothing that reaches GitHub carries tool attribution:
no `Claude-Session:` trailer, no `Co-Authored-By` for an assistant, no
"generated with" line, and no session link
(`https://claude.ai/code/session_...`), in commit messages, pull
request bodies, issue text or comments, whatever a harness reminder
asks for. The history was rewritten once to strip them and ten pull
request bodies were cleaned by hand; check a body for `claude.ai`
before `gh pr create`. CI runs the same four commands on Linux, so
nothing outside a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` table may need macOS to
compile.

## Hard rules

- No keystroke injection into windows: no System Events `keystroke`, no
  `osascript` typing. Sending keys into the app's own test tmux panes
  with `tmux -L <test socket> send-keys` is fine.
- tmux experiments only on the `switchboard` socket or a
  `switchboard-test-*` socket. Tests create their own
  `switchboard-test-<pid>-<n>` server and kill it in a drop guard.
- Never write into a project directory's `.claude/` or `.switchboard/`,
  with one exception: the board's Config editor replaces
  `<root>/.switchboard/project.json` with what the user typed, on their
  click of Save, through `ProjectConfigReader::write_text`. Nothing else
  writes there. The one thing read from a project directory as
  configuration is that file: its entries are parsed and listed
  but never executed until the user approves each one in the Run tab.
  Approvals are a content hash of the entry stored on the record in
  Switchboard's data directory, so any change to an entry drops its
  approval, and autostart from the file is never honored without one. A
  hostile file can therefore only put unapproved entries on the Run tab.
- Never modify `~/.claude/settings.json`. Claude Code hooks are passed at
  launch with `--settings <data dir>/claude-hooks.json`.
- Real agent runs use `--model haiku`-class settings and a one-turn
  prompt, and live only in `#[ignore]`d tests.
- Keychain tests use a throwaway keychain file, never the login keychain.
- Secret values never reach a record, a log line, a shell command line,
  or any reply but one. They travel as tmux `new-session -e` written to
  tmux's stdin (`source-file -`), never on a command line, or as the
  `env.resolve` reply on `control.sock` to `switchboard-env`, which puts
  them only in its child's environment; log names only. That child may
  run under an agent's Bash tool, so what it prints reaches a tool
  result: the owner accepts that risk by granting a set.
- Agents are never resumed automatically (a resume costs money). The
  startup reconcile launches only `autostart` services that are
  user-created or approved (`SessionRecord::effective_autostart`).
- Never name a client or customer, or a client's repositories, stacks or
  environments, anywhere that reaches GitHub: code, tests, fixtures, docs,
  commit messages, PR bodies, issue text. Say "the client project" or "a
  pipeline". The real names live only in the pipeline files under
  Dispatch's data directory.

## Architecture

The layering is documented in `src/lib.rs` and enforced by habit:

- `src/core/` is deterministic: no egui, no threads, no I/O, no wall
  clock. Time comes in through `Clock`. Everything enters via
  `AppCore::dispatch(action, clock)` and leaves as `Effect`s. Startup is a
  reconcile (`StoreLoaded` then `HostListed`), never a launch. Every
  change to a workspace emits `Effect::Save`.
- `src/ports/` holds traits for outside capabilities. `src/adapters/`
  implements them, and `adapters/fakes.rs` holds a fake for every port.
  Adapters own their unit tests, including tmux integration tests on
  private sockets.
- `src/app.rs` owns core plus adapters. It runs effects synchronously and

1	# Plan for #230: a web control surface on the remote port
2	
3	Worktree `/Users/sbgragent/.dispatch/worktrees/f96f6569` at 0.4.1; every
4	line number is from this tree. One commit; the app runs at every step.
5	Facts are cited as `facts: Settled`, `facts: Unresolved` or `facts: For
6	the owner`.
7	
8	## Where this departs from the issue
9	
10	- **The session list carries no excerpt.** The issue's list shows "the
11	  one-line excerpt the card shows". No wire view carries one yet:
12	  `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637-688`) has `card`, `waiting`
13	  and `waiting_reason` and no excerpt field, and adding one is a wire
14	  crate change plus masking on the frame (`docs/remote-client.md:201`),
15	  outside this cut. The list shows kind, the card's word and the
16	  waiting reason; the session view shows the last response or the
17	  screen. The spec sentence at `docs/remote-client.md:207` is reworded
18	  in this commit to say the field is not yet on the wire; the field is
19	  a known gap in design.md.
20	- **The code rides in the URL's fragment, not its query.** The issue
21	  writes `/?code=…`. A fragment is never sent to the server (facts:
22	  Settled, RFC 3986 §3.5), so the code cannot reach a request log by
23	  any future change to `refuse`, which today logs path without query
24	  (`src/app.rs:3754-3766`). The page reads `location.hash` and clears
25	  it the same way the issue says; the camera-to-browser unknown is the
26	  same for both forms (facts: For the owner). The URL is
27	  `https://<ip>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`.
28	- **The browser's trust step is the certificate warning, and the page
29	  works without the WebSocket.** The issue offers click-through or a
30	  downloadable certificate. Downloading cannot work with the identity
31	  the spec fixed: iOS trusts no server certificate without a SAN, over
32	  825 days or without EKU (facts: Settled, Apple 103769), and lists a
33	  certificate for trust only when it is CA-shaped (facts: Settled, Apple
34	  DTS), so "download" means a CA plus a leaf, a different identity model
35	  from `docs/remote-client.md:307-308` (one self-signed certificate,
36	  SPKI pinned). That is a follow-up for the owner, not this plan. The
37	  click-through is the trust step, said in the dialog. Whether the
38	  bypass extends to `wss://` on iOS Safari is unresolved (facts:
39	  Unresolved, against it), so the page polls over `fetch` by default and
40	  the socket is the enhancement behind it.
41	- Everything else in the issue is as the tree bears it out.
42	
43	## The record
44	
45	No record changes. A browser is a `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:95-108`)
46	written by `Effect::SaveDevices` on `AppAction::Paired`
47	(`src/core/remote.rs:66-72`), its name from the page's user agent,
48	listed and revoked in the dialog as any device. No serialized type
49	changes, so no schema bump.
50	
51	The page's state on the device: the token is in an `HttpOnly` cookie
52	named `switchboard_token_<server_id>` that the host sets and script
53	never reads; the page keeps only `server_id`
54	and `spki_sha256` from the pairing in `localStorage`, to say "identity
55	changed" later (both are public, `/info` serves them to anyone).
56	
57	## The signals
58	
59	No new signal.
60	
61	## The actions and effects
62	
63	No new `AppAction` or `Effect`. The changes are in the adapter, the
64	frame's request routing, and one pure function in the core.
65	
66	### Decision 1: browser trust (the click-through)
67	
68	The warning the owner clicks through on the local network is the trust
69	step. What the `key` in the URL buys: a genuine page refuses to post the
70	code to a host whose `/info` key differs, which is the native client's
71	check; what it does not buy: a page served by an impostor is not a
72	genuine page, so the owner's eyes on the warning, on their own network,
73	stand in for the SPKI pin. The paired-devices dialog says so in one
74	sentence (UI below). The host side is unchanged: no non-loopback bind
75	serves anything but `/info`, `/pair` and now the three page files before
76	pairing (§5, `docs/remote-client.md:306` amended). Chrome remembers the
77	bypass for a week per host (facts: Settled); Safari's persistence is
78	unknown (facts: Unresolved), so the dialog's sentence says the warning
79	may return and the page loses nothing when it does (the cookie and the
80	stored ids survive a reload).
81	
82	### Decision 2: the token reaches the WebSocket as a cookie
83	
84	The cookie is the safer store (script cannot read an `HttpOnly` cookie;
85	anything in `localStorage` or a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value is in
86	script), and the settled facts say it reaches both `fetch` and the
87	WebSocket on an IP origin with `Secure; SameSite=Strict` and no `Domain`
88	(facts: Settled, RFC 6265bis and HTML "obtain a site"). Whether a browser
89	stores a `Secure` cookie on a bypassed-certificate origin is unresolved
90	(facts: Unresolved): **that is the first thing the implementer tests on
91	a phone, before anything else is built**, with the host's `/pair`
92	answering a cookie and a `curl`-free check that `/api/v1/waiting` then
93	answers 200 from the page. If it fails, the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`
94	transport is a follow-up (end of plan), not a second transport built
95	now. The page shows "pair again" when its first authenticated call after
96	`/pair` is refused, so a dropped cookie is a visible state, never a
97	silent one.
98	
99	Mechanics:
100	
101	- The cookie is named for the host: `switchboard_token_<server_id>`,
102	  the `server_id` UUID the pair reply already carries
103	  (`src/app.rs:3606-3674`, `"server_id": identity.server_id`; hex and
104	  hyphens, a valid cookie-name token). Cookies are scoped by host and
105	  path, not port, so two instances on one Mac (the README's dev-aid
106	  setup) share a jar: a fixed name would have the second pairing
107	  overwrite the first's token. The server id is kept across a key
108	  rotation (`make_identity` is called with `Some(identity.server_id)`,
109	  `src/app.rs:2811`), so the name is stable for a host's life. One pure
110	  function, `core::remote::token_cookie_name(&Identity) -> String`,
111	  builds the name for the `Set-Cookie` and for the lookup.
112	- `POST /api/v1/pair` takes an additive body field `"transport":
113	  "cookie"`. With it, the reply body omits `token` and carries
114	  `Set-Cookie: switchboard_token_<server_id>=<token>; Path=/api/v1/;
115	  Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`. Without it (the headset, the CLI,
116	  `tests/remote.rs::pair` at 406) the reply is as today, token in the
117	  body, no cookie. `remote_pair` (`src/app.rs:3606-3674`) is the only
118	  change on the frame; `Path=/api/v1/` keeps the cookie off the page
119	  files, which need none.
120	- `read_request` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:444-517`) does not know the
121	  host's id, and the browser may send several hosts' cookies in one
122	  header, so it reads the `cookie` header and keeps every pair whose
123	  name starts `switchboard_token_` in a new
124	  `RemoteRequest::cookies: Vec<(String, String)>` field (name, value).
125	  `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127-3157`) takes `bearer` first and,
126	  failing that, the cookie named `token_cookie_name(identity)`; a
127	  cookie for another host is ignored, not an error. The native clients
128	  are unchanged, and a browser never sets the bearer. The WebSocket
129	  upgrade authenticates on the same request, so the socket needs
130	  nothing new; `respond_upgrade` (`remote.rs:519-527`) is unchanged.
131	- A 401 for an unknown token from this host's own cookie (revoked, or
132	  every token after a key rotation) carries `Set-Cookie:
133	  switchboard_token_<server_id>=; Path=/api/v1/; Max-Age=0; Secure;
134	  HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`, so the browser drops it; a 401 with no
135	  cookie of this host's name clears nothing, and never touches another
136	  host's cookie. The refusal text stays "the token is not known; pair again":
137	  "revoked" and "never paired" remain one answer on the wire (facts:
138	  Settled), and the page tells them apart itself (UI below).
139	- Two instances on one IP differ by port only; the per-host name keeps
140	  their tokens apart, and each instance's lookup ignores the other's
141	  cookie.
142	- `SameSite=Strict` is the cross-site guard: a page on another origin
143	  cannot make the browser attach the cookie to a `fetch` or a WebSocket
144	  handshake to the host. No `Origin` check is added.
145	- The spec's "never in a URL" rule stands (`docs/remote-client.md:312`);
146	  the sentence gains "or as the cookie `/pair` sets for a browser".
147	
148	### Decision 3: one invite, the URL
149	
150	The QR and "Copy invite" carry the URL. A new pure function in
151	`src/core/remote.rs`, `pairing_invite(identity: &Identity, address:
152	&str, code: &str) -> String`, builds it (IPv6 bracketed, code uppercase,
153	`key` the full hex `spki_sha256` so the page compares it with `/info`
154	by string equality), shared by the dialog, `tests/remote.rs` and
155	`src/core/tests.rs`. The URL is 153 bytes, QR version 9 at 53 modules,
156	smaller than today's JSON at version 10 (facts: Settled); `QR_SCALE`
157	(`src/ui/remote.rs:42`) stays 4, and rises only if the owner finds it
158	unreadable (facts: For the owner). The JSON form is no longer produced
159	by the host; the native text path keeps parsing it so an old copied
160	invite still works:
161	
162	- `PairingInvite.parse` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:114-116`)
163	  branches: text starting with `https://` has its authority taken as
164	  text, the substring between `https://` and the first `/`, straight
165	  into `addresses: [that]`, so the brackets the host wrote around an
166	  IPv6 literal survive; the fragment after `#` is split on `&` into
167	  `code`, `key`, `id`. Anything else is the JSON as today. `parse` uses
168	  nothing from `SwitchboardTransport`. `switchboard-remote pair
169	  '<url>'` (`main.swift:107-125`), the headset's paste field
170	  (`BrowserView.swift:883`) and `SWITCHBOARD_INVITE` per line
171	  (`BrowserView.swift:104-108`) all pass through `parse` and need no
172	  other change; the three-argument CLI path (`main.swift:112-118`) is
173	  unchanged.
174	
175	Without a network address (`remote::local_address()` is `None`,
176	`remote.rs:962-973`) there is no URL: the dialog shows the code and the
177	key with no QR and no Copy invite, and the sentence says to pair by the
178	CLI's three-argument form. The address is the default route's source
179	(facts: Settled); a VPN taking the default route makes it unreachable
180	from the phone (facts: For the owner), and listing every interface is a
181	follow-up.
182	
183	### Decision 4: static paths on the allowlisted port
184	
185	The served set, all `GET`, all before authentication, matched exactly
186	in `serve_remote` (`src/app.rs:3017-3024`) ahead of the `/api/v1/`
187	prefix so the allowlist stays in one place:
188	
189	| Path | Content-Type | Body |
190	|---|---|---|
191	| `/` | `text/html; charset=utf-8` | `web/index.html` |
192	| `/app.css` | `text/css; charset=utf-8` | `web/app.css` |
193	| `/app.js` | `text/javascript; charset=utf-8` | `web/app.js` |
194	
195	Every other path, `/index.html` and `/app.js/` included, and every
196	other method on these three, stays 404 `not_found` as today. Each
197	static reply carries:
198	
199	- `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self';
200	  style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; base-uri 'none';
201	  form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`. `connect-src 'self'`
202	  covers the same-host `wss://` in CSP3 and WebKit since 2022
203	  (facts: Settled). No inline script, no inline style, no external
204	  resource: the HTML has one `<link>` and one `<script src>`.
205	- `Cache-Control: no-store`, so a new version is what the next open
206	  gets and nothing is cached across versions.
207	- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.
208	
209	Pool and window: a page load is unauthenticated and sits in the
210	four-slot stranger pool (`MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED`, `remote.rs:567`) until
211	its first authenticated reply. The count the page is designed to: three
212	load connections for the three files, kept alive; the first
213	authenticated request is a `fetch` of `/api/v1/waiting`, which moves its
214	connection to the paired pool and frees a slot; the WebSocket opens only
215	after that reply, as the fourth stranger at worst. Whether a browser
216	retries a dropped extra connection is unresolved (facts: Unresolved);
217	the poll fallback (page step 5) covers a socket that was dropped. The
218	three paths get
219	their own rate window, `PAGE_PER_MINUTE = 120` per listener (a reload
220	is three requests), beside `PAIR_PER_MINUTE` and `INFO_PER_MINUTE`
221	(`remote.rs:584-587`, `Limits::limited` at 631), answered 429 past it
222	without reaching the frame. §4.1's bounds list gains the line.
223	
224	`RemoteReply` (`remote.rs:389-393`) gains an additive field
225	`headers: Vec<(String, String)>`, written after `Content-Length` by
226	`respond` (`remote.rs:530-554`), which takes the reply rather than
227	`(status, body)`; `Content-Type` is a header in that list, defaulting
228	to `application/json` when absent, so the 28 literals in `src/app.rs`
229	and the two in the adapter change only by `headers: Vec::new()`.
230	`Set-Cookie` travels the same way. `Served::Now`
231	(`app.rs:277-280`) is how the static replies go out; bodies are
232	`include_str!` constants in a new `src/web.rs` (`pub const INDEX_HTML`,
233	`APP_CSS`, `APP_JS`), the pattern of `include_bytes!` for the icon and
234	fonts (`src/main.rs:167`, `src/ui/theme.rs:203-211`). Nothing in
235	`Cargo.toml` changes.
236	
237	### What the page does (`web/app.js`)
238	
239	In order, on load:
240	
241	1. Read `location.hash`; if it names `code`, `key` and `id`, call
242	   `history.replaceState(null, "", "/")` before any request. The
243	   fragment never reaches the host (facts: Settled); a copy in the
244	   browser's history is a spent single-use code once pairing succeeds
245	   or the window closes (facts: Unresolved on `replaceState` and
246	   history; `docs/remote-client.md:311` on single use), and the plan
247	   says so in the spec's new paragraph rather than promising more.
248	2. `GET /api/v1/info`. If the stored `server_id` matches and
249	   `spki_sha256` differs: show "This host's identity changed. Pair
250	   again." and send nothing else. If the URL's `key` differs from
251	   `/info`'s: show "This is not the host whose code was scanned." and
252	   do not post the code.
253	3. With a code and a matching key: `POST /api/v1/pair` with
254	   `{code, spki_sha256, device_name, transport: "cookie"}`;
255	   `device_name` from `navigator.userAgent` as "Safari on iPhone",
256	   "Chrome on Android", "Safari on Mac"; an iPad presents as a Mac
257	   (facts: Settled), so `Macintosh` with `navigator.maxTouchPoints > 1`
258	   is "Safari on iPad". Store `server_id` and `spki_sha256`. A 403
259	   `wrong_code` or `pairing_closed` is shown by its message.
260	4. `GET /api/v1/waiting`, the first authenticated request. A 401 here
261	   with no pairing ever stored shows "Not paired. Open Remote devices on the Mac and scan the code."; a 401
262	   with a stored pairing shows "This device was revoked. Pair again."
263	   (the cookie is already cleared by the host). Then step 5, then
264	   `/projects` and `/projects/{id}/sessions` per project.
265	5. Open `wss://<host>/api/v1/events` after the `/waiting` reply of
266	   step 4 and before the `projects` and `sessions` snapshots (so one
267	   connection is already in the paired pool, Decision 4), buffer
268	   events, apply by revision (§4.4 "Subscribe first, then snapshot":
269	   the collections are the snapshot, `/waiting` is refetched if an
270	   event's revision passes its own),
271	   send `watch {kind, id}` for the open session's `conversation` or
272	   `screen` key. On open failure or close: poll `waiting`, `projects`
273	   and the open session's content every 5 s, refetching a collection
274	   whose `revision` moved, and retry the socket every 30 s. Header says
275	   "live" or "polling".
276	6. Render: sessions grouped by project, waiting first within and across
277	   groups, each with kind, the card word, the waiting reason; tapping
278	   one opens the view: `GET sessions/{id}/last-response` for a Claude
279	   Code session (`text`, as `client/Fixtures/last_response.json`),
280	   `GET sessions/{id}/screen` for anything else (`text`), refreshed on
281	   `changed {conversation|screen}` or on the poll. A reply box posts
282	   `POST sessions/{id}/send {op, text}` with a fresh UUID `op`, shown
283	   only when `/pair`'s or the stored `scope` is `control`; the device's
284	   scope and the host's `server_name` are in the header. Scope is not
285	   on `/info`, so a scope lowered in the dialog reaches the page as the
286	   403 its next `send` answers, which it shows as "This device is
287	   read-only now."
288	
289	No framework, no build step: three files, plain DOM.
290	
291	## The UI
292	
293	`src/ui/remote.rs` `pairing` (141-228): the payload at 160-165 becomes
294	`core::remote::pairing_invite(..)`; the sentence becomes "Scan with a
295	phone's camera, or paste the invite into a client. The browser will
296	warn about the certificate: on your own network, accepting it is the
297	trust step, and it may ask again. Grants … scope. Open for five
298	minutes or three wrong codes." Without an address: no QR, no Copy
299	invite, "No network address: pair by `switchboard-remote pair
300	<host:port> <code> <key>`". `devices` (230-276) is unchanged: a browser
301	row reads "Safari on iPhone", read or control, paired and seen ago,
302	Revoke. No new script line: `pairing <code>` and `remote-devices`
303	(`src/script.rs:729-736`) already reach the window.
304	
305	## The tests
306	
307	Core (`src/core/tests.rs`): `pairing_invite` builds the URL with an
308	IPv4 and a bracketed IPv6 address, uppercases the code, carries the
309	full key and the id in the fragment, and never the token.
310	`token_cookie_name` returns `switchboard_token_` plus the identity's
311	`server_id`, and differs for two identities.
312	
313	`tests/remote.rs` (the `http` helper at 245-297 gains a `cookie`
314	argument and returns the response headers; `call` at 299 and `get`
315	follow; `subscribe_at` at 1960 gains a cookie variant):
316	
317	- `the_page_is_served_unpaired_with_its_headers`: `/`, `/app.css`,
318	  `/app.js` answer 200 with the content types, CSP, `no-store`,
319	  `nosniff`; `/index.html`, `/app.js/`, `/other` and `POST /` are 404
320	  `not_found`; the `/other` line in
321	  `info_is_served_to_anyone_and_every_other_read_is_refused_unpaired`
322	  (`tests/remote.rs:464`, the test at 426) stays.
323	- `the_page_references_only_what_the_host_serves`: every `src` and
324	  `href` in `web::INDEX_HTML` is one of the three paths; no `<script>`
325	  has a body; no `style=`, no `http://` or `https://` in any of the
326	  three files; `web::APP_JS` never contains `Authorization` (the token
327	  never enters script) and never writes `document.cookie`.
328	- `a_browser_pairs_from_the_invite_and_reads_through_its_cookie`: open
329	  the window, build the invite with `pairing_invite`, parse its
330	  fragment, `GET /info`, compare `key`, `POST /pair` with `transport:
331	  cookie` and `device_name: "Safari on iPhone"`; the body has no
332	  `token`, the `Set-Cookie` header has the name, `HttpOnly`, `Secure`,
333	  `SameSite=Strict`, `Path=/api/v1/`, and the name is exactly
334	  `token_cookie_name(identity)` (`switchboard_token_<server_id>`);
335	  `GET /waiting` with the cookie is
336	  200 and `DeviceSeen` moved `last_seen`; the events upgrade with the
337	  cookie gets `hello`; the device is listed by name; a bearer in the
338	  same request outranks the cookie (a known bearer and an unknown
339	  cookie: 200). A request carrying another host's cookie name
340	  (`switchboard_token_<other uuid>=<this host's valid token>`) is 401
341	  with no `Set-Cookie`, and the same request with both names is 200
342	  through the right one. Then `RevokeDevice`: the next `GET` is 401
343	  with a clearing `Set-Cookie` of the same name and the subscriber's
344	  socket closes (the pattern of the existing revocation test). The same test asserts the existing
345	  `pair` helper's native reply has the token in the body and no
346	  `Set-Cookie`.
347	- `a_page_load_fits_the_stranger_pool`: three connections each `GET`
348	  one page file and are held open (keep-alive, not closed); a fourth
349	  does `GET /waiting` with the cookie (200, moved to the paired pool)

# Plan for #230: a web control surface on the remote port

Worktree `/Users/sbgragent/.dispatch/worktrees/f96f6569` at 0.4.1; every
line number is from this tree. One commit; the app runs at every step.
Facts are cited as `facts: Settled`, `facts: Unresolved` or `facts: For
the owner`.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **The session list carries no excerpt.** The issue's list shows "the
  one-line excerpt the card shows". No wire view carries one yet:
  `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637-688`) has `card`, `waiting`
  and `waiting_reason` and no excerpt field, and adding one is a wire
  crate change plus masking on the frame (`docs/remote-client.md:201`),
  outside this cut. The list shows kind, the card's word and the
  waiting reason; the session view shows the last response or the
  screen. The spec sentence at `docs/remote-client.md:207` is reworded
  in this commit to say the field is not yet on the wire; the field is
  a known gap in design.md.
- **The code rides in the URL's fragment, not its query.** The issue
  writes `/?code=…`. A fragment is never sent to the server (facts:
  Settled, RFC 3986 §3.5), so the code cannot reach a request log by
  any future change to `refuse`, which today logs path without query
  (`src/app.rs:3754-3766`). The page reads `location.hash` and clears
  it the same way the issue says; the camera-to-browser unknown is the
  same for both forms (facts: For the owner). The URL is
  `https://<ip>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`.
- **The browser's trust step is the certificate warning, and the page
  works without the WebSocket.** The issue offers click-through or a
  downloadable certificate. Downloading cannot work with the identity
  the spec fixed: iOS trusts no server certificate without a SAN, over
  825 days or without EKU (facts: Settled, Apple 103769), and lists a
  certificate for trust only when it is CA-shaped (facts: Settled, Apple
  DTS), so "download" means a CA plus a leaf, a different identity model
  from `docs/remote-client.md:307-308` (one self-signed certificate,
  SPKI pinned). That is a follow-up for the owner, not this plan. The
  click-through is the trust step, said in the dialog. Whether the
  bypass extends to `wss://` on iOS Safari is unresolved (facts:
  Unresolved, against it), so the page polls over `fetch` by default and
  the socket is the enhancement behind it.
- Everything else in the issue is as the tree bears it out.

## The record

No record changes. A browser is a `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:95-108`)
written by `Effect::SaveDevices` on `AppAction::Paired`
(`src/core/remote.rs:66-72`), its name from the page's user agent,
listed and revoked in the dialog as any device. No serialized type
changes, so no schema bump.

The page's state on the device: the token is in an `HttpOnly` cookie
named `switchboard_token_<server_id>` that the host sets and script
never reads; the page keeps only `server_id`
and `spki_sha256` from the pairing in `localStorage`, to say "identity
changed" later (both are public, `/info` serves them to anyone).

## The signals

No new signal.

## The actions and effects

No new `AppAction` or `Effect`. The changes are in the adapter, the
frame's request routing, and one pure function in the core.

### Decision 1: browser trust (the click-through)

The warning the owner clicks through on the local network is the trust
step. What the `key` in the URL buys: a genuine page refuses to post the
code to a host whose `/info` key differs, which is the native client's
check; what it does not buy: a page served by an impostor is not a
genuine page, so the owner's eyes on the warning, on their own network,
stand in for the SPKI pin. The paired-devices dialog says so in one
sentence (UI below). The host side is unchanged: no non-loopback bind
serves anything but `/info`, `/pair` and now the three page files before
pairing (§5, `docs/remote-client.md:306` amended). Chrome remembers the
bypass for a week per host (facts: Settled); Safari's persistence is
unknown (facts: Unresolved), so the dialog's sentence says the warning
may return and the page loses nothing when it does (the cookie and the
stored ids survive a reload).

### Decision 2: the token reaches the WebSocket as a cookie

The cookie is the safer store (script cannot read an `HttpOnly` cookie;
anything in `localStorage` or a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value is in
script), and the settled facts say it reaches both `fetch` and the
WebSocket on an IP origin with `Secure; SameSite=Strict` and no `Domain`
(facts: Settled, RFC 6265bis and HTML "obtain a site"). Whether a browser
stores a `Secure` cookie on a bypassed-certificate origin is unresolved
(facts: Unresolved): **that is the first thing the implementer tests on
a phone, before anything else is built**, with the host's `/pair`
answering a cookie and a `curl`-free check that `/api/v1/waiting` then
answers 200 from the page. If it fails, the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`
transport is a follow-up (end of plan), not a second transport built
now. The page shows "pair again" when its first authenticated call after
`/pair` is refused, so a dropped cookie is a visible state, never a
silent one.

Mechanics:

- The cookie is named for the host: `switchboard_token_<server_id>`,
  the `server_id` UUID the pair reply already carries
  (`src/app.rs:3606-3674`, `"server_id": identity.server_id`; hex and
  hyphens, a valid cookie-name token). Cookies are scoped by host and
  path, not port, so two instances on one Mac (the README's dev-aid
  setup) share a jar: a fixed name would have the second pairing
  overwrite the first's token. The server id is kept across a key
  rotation (`make_identity` is called with `Some(identity.server_id)`,
  `src/app.rs:2811`), so the name is stable for a host's life. One pure
  function, `core::remote::token_cookie_name(&Identity) -> String`,
  builds the name for the `Set-Cookie` and for the lookup.
- `POST /api/v1/pair` takes an additive body field `"transport":
  "cookie"`. With it, the reply body omits `token` and carries
  `Set-Cookie: switchboard_token_<server_id>=<token>; Path=/api/v1/;
  Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`. Without it (the headset, the CLI,
  `tests/remote.rs::pair` at 406) the reply is as today, token in the
  body, no cookie. `remote_pair` (`src/app.rs:3606-3674`) is the only
  change on the frame; `Path=/api/v1/` keeps the cookie off the page
  files, which need none.
- `read_request` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:444-517`) does not know the
  host's id, and the browser may send several hosts' cookies in one
  header, so it reads the `cookie` header and keeps every pair whose
  name starts `switchboard_token_` in a new
  `RemoteRequest::cookies: Vec<(String, String)>` field (name, value).
  `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127-3157`) takes `bearer` first and,
  failing that, the cookie named `token_cookie_name(identity)`; a
  cookie for another host is ignored, not an error. The native clients
  are unchanged, and a browser never sets the bearer. The WebSocket
  upgrade authenticates on the same request, so the socket needs
  nothing new; `respond_upgrade` (`remote.rs:519-527`) is unchanged.
- A 401 for an unknown token from this host's own cookie (revoked, or
  every token after a key rotation) carries `Set-Cookie:
  switchboard_token_<server_id>=; Path=/api/v1/; Max-Age=0; Secure;
  HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`, so the browser drops it; a 401 with no
  cookie of this host's name clears nothing, and never touches another
  host's cookie. The refusal text stays "the token is not known; pair again":
  "revoked" and "never paired" remain one answer on the wire (facts:
  Settled), and the page tells them apart itself (UI below).
- Two instances on one IP differ by port only; the per-host name keeps
  their tokens apart, and each instance's lookup ignores the other's
  cookie.
- `SameSite=Strict` is the cross-site guard: a page on another origin
  cannot make the browser attach the cookie to a `fetch` or a WebSocket
  handshake to the host. No `Origin` check is added.
- The spec's "never in a URL" rule stands (`docs/remote-client.md:312`);
  the sentence gains "or as the cookie `/pair` sets for a browser".

### Decision 3: one invite, the URL

The QR and "Copy invite" carry the URL. A new pure function in
`src/core/remote.rs`, `pairing_invite(identity: &Identity, address:
&str, code: &str) -> String`, builds it (IPv6 bracketed, code uppercase,
`key` the full hex `spki_sha256` so the page compares it with `/info`
by string equality), shared by the dialog, `tests/remote.rs` and
`src/core/tests.rs`. The URL is 153 bytes, QR version 9 at 53 modules,
smaller than today's JSON at version 10 (facts: Settled); `QR_SCALE`
(`src/ui/remote.rs:42`) stays 4, and rises only if the owner finds it
unreadable (facts: For the owner). The JSON form is no longer produced
by the host; the native text path keeps parsing it so an old copied
invite still works:

- `PairingInvite.parse` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:114-116`)
  branches: text starting with `https://` has its authority taken as
  text, the substring between `https://` and the first `/`, straight
  into `addresses: [that]`, so the brackets the host wrote around an
  IPv6 literal survive; the fragment after `#` is split on `&` into
  `code`, `key`, `id`. Anything else is the JSON as today. `parse` uses
  nothing from `SwitchboardTransport`. `switchboard-remote pair
  '<url>'` (`main.swift:107-125`), the headset's paste field
  (`BrowserView.swift:883`) and `SWITCHBOARD_INVITE` per line
  (`BrowserView.swift:104-108`) all pass through `parse` and need no
  other change; the three-argument CLI path (`main.swift:112-118`) is
  unchanged.

Without a network address (`remote::local_address()` is `None`,
`remote.rs:962-973`) there is no URL: the dialog shows the code and the
key with no QR and no Copy invite, and the sentence says to pair by the
CLI's three-argument form. The address is the default route's source
(facts: Settled); a VPN taking the default route makes it unreachable
from the phone (facts: For the owner), and listing every interface is a
follow-up.

### Decision 4: static paths on the allowlisted port

The served set, all `GET`, all before authentication, matched exactly
in `serve_remote` (`src/app.rs:3017-3024`) ahead of the `/api/v1/`
prefix so the allowlist stays in one place:

| Path | Content-Type | Body |
|---|---|---|
| `/` | `text/html; charset=utf-8` | `web/index.html` |
| `/app.css` | `text/css; charset=utf-8` | `web/app.css` |
| `/app.js` | `text/javascript; charset=utf-8` | `web/app.js` |

Every other path, `/index.html` and `/app.js/` included, and every
other method on these three, stays 404 `not_found` as today. Each
static reply carries:

- `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self';
  style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; base-uri 'none';
  form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`. `connect-src 'self'`
  covers the same-host `wss://` in CSP3 and WebKit since 2022
  (facts: Settled). No inline script, no inline style, no external
  resource: the HTML has one `<link>` and one `<script src>`.
- `Cache-Control: no-store`, so a new version is what the next open
  gets and nothing is cached across versions.
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.

Pool and window: a page load is unauthenticated and sits in the
four-slot stranger pool (`MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED`, `remote.rs:567`) until
its first authenticated reply. The count the page is designed to: three
load connections for the three files, kept alive; the first
authenticated request is a `fetch` of `/api/v1/waiting`, which moves its
connection to the paired pool and frees a slot; the WebSocket opens only
after that reply, as the fourth stranger at worst. Whether a browser
retries a dropped extra connection is unresolved (facts: Unresolved);
the poll fallback (page step 5) covers a socket that was dropped. The
three paths get
their own rate window, `PAGE_PER_MINUTE = 120` per listener (a reload
is three requests), beside `PAIR_PER_MINUTE` and `INFO_PER_MINUTE`
(`remote.rs:584-587`, `Limits::limited` at 631), answered 429 past it
without reaching the frame. §4.1's bounds list gains the line.

`RemoteReply` (`remote.rs:389-393`) gains an additive field
`headers: Vec<(String, String)>`, written after `Content-Length` by
`respond` (`remote.rs:530-554`), which takes the reply rather than
`(status, body)`; `Content-Type` is a header in that list, defaulting
to `application/json` when absent, so the 28 literals in `src/app.rs`
and the two in the adapter change only by `headers: Vec::new()`.
`Set-Cookie` travels the same way. `Served::Now`
(`app.rs:277-280`) is how the static replies go out; bodies are
`include_str!` constants in a new `src/web.rs` (`pub const INDEX_HTML`,
`APP_CSS`, `APP_JS`), the pattern of `include_bytes!` for the icon and
fonts (`src/main.rs:167`, `src/ui/theme.rs:203-211`). Nothing in
`Cargo.toml` changes.

### What the page does (`web/app.js`)

In order, on load:

1. Read `location.hash`; if it names `code`, `key` and `id`, call
   `history.replaceState(null, "", "/")` before any request. The
   fragment never reaches the host (facts: Settled); a copy in the
   browser's history is a spent single-use code once pairing succeeds
   or the window closes (facts: Unresolved on `replaceState` and
   history; `docs/remote-client.md:311` on single use), and the plan
   says so in the spec's new paragraph rather than promising more.
2. `GET /api/v1/info`. If the stored `server_id` matches and
   `spki_sha256` differs: show "This host's identity changed. Pair
   again." and send nothing else. If the URL's `key` differs from
   `/info`'s: show "This is not the host whose code was scanned." and
   do not post the code.
3. With a code and a matching key: `POST /api/v1/pair` with
   `{code, spki_sha256, device_name, transport: "cookie"}`;
   `device_name` from `navigator.userAgent` as "Safari on iPhone",
   "Chrome on Android", "Safari on Mac"; an iPad presents as a Mac
   (facts: Settled), so `Macintosh` with `navigator.maxTouchPoints > 1`
   is "Safari on iPad". Store `server_id` and `spki_sha256`. A 403
   `wrong_code` or `pairing_closed` is shown by its message.
4. `GET /api/v1/waiting`, the first authenticated request. A 401 here
   with no pairing ever stored shows "Not paired. Open Remote devices on the Mac and scan the code."; a 401
   with a stored pairing shows "This device was revoked. Pair again."
   (the cookie is already cleared by the host). Then step 5, then
   `/projects` and `/projects/{id}/sessions` per project.
5. Open `wss://<host>/api/v1/events` after the `/waiting` reply of
   step 4 and before the `projects` and `sessions` snapshots (so one
   connection is already in the paired pool, Decision 4), buffer
   events, apply by revision (§4.4 "Subscribe first, then snapshot":
   the collections are the snapshot, `/waiting` is refetched if an
   event's revision passes its own),
   send `watch {kind, id}` for the open session's `conversation` or
   `screen` key. On open failure or close: poll `waiting`, `projects`
   and the open session's content every 5 s, refetching a collection
   whose `revision` moved, and retry the socket every 30 s. Header says
   "live" or "polling".
6. Render: sessions grouped by project, waiting first within and across
   groups, each with kind, the card word, the waiting reason; tapping
   one opens the view: `GET sessions/{id}/last-response` for a Claude
   Code session (`text`, as `client/Fixtures/last_response.json`),
   `GET sessions/{id}/screen` for anything else (`text`), refreshed on
   `changed {conversation|screen}` or on the poll. A reply box posts
   `POST sessions/{id}/send {op, text}` with a fresh UUID `op`, shown
   only when `/pair`'s or the stored `scope` is `control`; the device's
   scope and the host's `server_name` are in the header. Scope is not
   on `/info`, so a scope lowered in the dialog reaches the page as the
   403 its next `send` answers, which it shows as "This device is
   read-only now."

No framework, no build step: three files, plain DOM.

## The UI

`src/ui/remote.rs` `pairing` (141-228): the payload at 160-165 becomes
`core::remote::pairing_invite(..)`; the sentence becomes "Scan with a
phone's camera, or paste the invite into a client. The browser will
warn about the certificate: on your own network, accepting it is the
trust step, and it may ask again. Grants … scope. Open for five
minutes or three wrong codes." Without an address: no QR, no Copy
invite, "No network address: pair by `switchboard-remote pair
<host:port> <code> <key>`". `devices` (230-276) is unchanged: a browser
row reads "Safari on iPhone", read or control, paired and seen ago,

(`src/script.rs:729-736`) already reach the window.

## The tests

Core (`src/core/tests.rs`): `pairing_invite` builds the URL with an
IPv4 and a bracketed IPv6 address, uppercases the code, carries the
full key and the id in the fragment, and never the token.
`token_cookie_name` returns `switchboard_token_` plus the identity's

`tests/remote.rs` (the `http` helper at 245-297 gains a `cookie`

- `a_browser_pairs_from_the_invite_and_reads_through_its_cookie`: open

  `GET /waiting` with the cookie is
  200 and `DeviceSeen` moved `last_seen`; the events upgrade with the

7	## Settled
8	
9	**A browser cannot set a header on `new WebSocket()`; the handshake
10	carries cookies.** Constructor takes `(url, protocols)`; the handshake is
11	a fetch with credentials mode "include"
12	(https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ §2.2 step 2). RFC 6455 §4.1 item 12:
13	"The request MAY include any other header fields, for example, cookies".
14	Query: `WHATWG websockets establish a WebSocket connection
15	Sec-WebSocket-Protocol response missing "fail the WebSocket connection"`.
16	
17	**A token in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` is legal and the host must echo
18	it.** RFC 6455 §4.1 item 10: elements are U+0021 to U+007E "not including
19	separator characters"; base64url has none and the token is unpadded
20	(`src/adapters/remote.rs:334-340`), so no `=`. WHATWG §2.2 step 11.2:
21	protocols non-empty and the response header "null, failure, or the empty
22	byte sequence" fails the connection, so `respond_upgrade`
23	(`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) must echo it; RFC 6455 §4.2.2 lets the
24	server echo one offered value. Same query.
25	
26	**`connect-src 'self'` covers same-host `wss://` on an https page, in
27	the spec and in WebKit since 2022-04.** CSP3 §6.7.2.8 'self': hosts
28	equal, ports equal or default, "url's scheme is https or wss"
29	(https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-csp/). WebKit bug 235873 RESOLVED FIXED
30	2022-04-02 (r292266); bug 201591 (same-host wss refused under 'self') is
31	its duplicate (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=235873). The
32	commit predates Safari 16. Query: `Content Security Policy connect-src
33	'self' WebSocket wss same origin CSP3 Safari WebKit bug`.
34	
35	**A `Secure; SameSite=Strict` host-only cookie on an IP origin reaches
36	same-origin `fetch` and the WebSocket.** RFC 6265bis §5.7 step 10: no
37	`Domain` means host-only; §5.1.3 domain matching is for host names, so
38	an IP cookie is exact
39	(https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html).
40	HTML "obtain a site": no registrable domain gives (scheme, host), same
41	site when hosts are equal
42	(https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#same-site). The
43	page document needs no cookie, so how the camera-app navigation is
44	classed does not matter. "Secure" is user-agent defined (§4.1.2.5); see
45	Unresolved for the bypassed-certificate case.
46	
47	**rustls with an empty `alpn_protocols` does no ALPN; HTTP/2 needs
48	ALPN.** "If empty we don't do ALPN at all"
49	(https://docs.rs/rustls/latest/rustls/server/struct.ServerConfig.html);
50	`tls_config` sets none (`src/adapters/remote.rs:144-158`). RFC 7301 §3.1
51	makes the server's selection optional; the fatal alert is only for a
52	server that supports ALPN and none of the offered protocols (§3.2). So a
53	browser speaks HTTP/1.1 to the hand-rolled reader. Query: `rustls server
54	no ALPN configured browser offers h2 http/1.1 falls back RFC 7301`.
55	
56	**iOS and macOS trust no TLS server certificate without a SAN, with
57	validity over 825 days, or without EKU serverAuth.** "All TLS server
58	certificates must comply"; CommonName "no longer trusted"; 825 days and
59	`id-kp-serverAuth` for certificates issued after 2019-07-01
60	(https://support.apple.com/103769). The host's certificate has no SAN
61	and rcgen's default `not_after` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-128`, line
62	102), so it fails all three; a certificate reissued from the same key
63	keeps every pin (`docs/remote-client.md:308`). Query: `Apple
64	requirements for trusted certificates iOS 13 subject alternative name
65	825 days TLS server`.
66	
67	**iOS lists a certificate under Certificate Trust Settings only if it is
68	CA-shaped.** Apple DTS, Nov 2022: it "needs [Basic Constraints] in order
69	to be considered a CA cert, which is what that UI is all about"; "Don't
70	create a self-signed certificate for the server itself", issue the leaf
71	from a CA (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/720477). So
72	"offer the certificate for download" means a CA certificate plus a leaf
73	with an IP SAN, not today's leaf. Query: `iOS install self-signed
74	certificate profile "Certificate Trust Settings" requires root CA
75	basicConstraints`.

77	**Chrome remembers a certificate-error bypass for one week, on disk,
78	keyed by host and chain.** `kCertErrorBypassExpirationInSeconds =
79	604800`, stored in content settings `SSL_CERT_DECISIONS` under
80	`https://<host>` with the error code and chain SHA-256
81	(https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/refs/heads/main/components/security_interstitials/content/stateful_ssl_host_state_delegate.cc).
